div.p: Federated Learning is a machine learning technique which trains models that is inside multiple edge devices and only sends model updates like gradients or weights instead of raw complete data to the central server. Edge Computing is a computing technique that processes data close to where it is generated, for example, in IoT devices instead of centralized cloud servers. Federated Learning with Edge Computing, also called as FLEC, allows decentralized patient data processing, helping in healthcare analytics. To observe temperature, heart rate, and SpO₂ levels, which is the oxygen level in blood, this study applies FLEC using simulated healthcare data activating alerts for any defects. A contrast study with Fog Computing, Cloud Computing, and Data Compression confirms that FLEC significantly reduces response time, which is the time taken for a system to react. FLEC decreases delays and reduces dependency on cloud while maintaining model accuracy and reducing loss by spreading upgrades across edge devices.

div.head: I.INTRODUCTION
div.p: The increased use of healthcare technology requires constant patient monitoring. Federated Learning with Edge Computing (FLEC) helps decentralized learning at the edge device, allowing quicker updates while holding privacy [3]. This study presents a FLEC-based system that notes vitals like temperature, heart rate, SpO₂ and triggers alerts for abnormal readings, allowing for on-time intervention. Using simulated ECG (Electrocardiogram is a test that tracks the activity of the heart) data, an analysis of response time comparing FLEC with Cloud Computing, Fog Computing, and Data Compression shows FLEC's efficiency in decreasing delays and being very efficient. In this way, FLEC allows quick responses for emergencies. Federated Learning with Edge Computing upgrades response times while preserving accuracy and privacy [20].

div.head: Role of IoT:
div.p: The Internet of Things (IoT) plays a crucial role here by connecting Iot devices like smartwatches and pulse oximeters to edge devices such as Raspberry Pi and portable medical devices. These edge devices collect and process patient data locally, reducing the dependency on cloud and improving decision-making [20]. This paper is structured as follows: I. Introduction, II. Problem Statement, III. Literature Review, IV. Methodology, V. Implementation, VI. Results, VII. Conclusion, Limitations and Future Scope, and VII. References.

div.head: II.PROBLEM-STATEMENT
div.p: Centralized structures like Cloud Computing are used in healthcare tracking [13]. Delays in emergency situations block real-time observing as well as quick decision-making. Network traffic and scalability issues also increase by depending on cloud. Already existing methods find it difficult to balance processing, being private and being efficient all at once. Increase in cloud computing's response times delay medical involvement, while data communication risks increase security concerns. Centralized systems are prone to network failures and scalability issues. Fog Computing, a decentralized model, still faces challenges like network failures, latency, and resource limitations [14]. Data compression, used to reduce the bandwidth needed for transmitting large healthcare datasets, has its own problems like data loss, latency and computational overhead. For fast, secure, and privacy-enabled healthcare analytics, a decentralized and improved solution is needed especially for observing critical patients [11].

III. LITERATURE REVIEW Federated learning's challenges and applications like data heterogeneity, communication overhead, and privacy concerns are surveyed [1]. Federated learning's usage in edge computing, and identifying key problems and solutions related to efficiency, security, and system optimization are done [3]. A secure personal authentication method for fog devices using multimodal rank-level fusion to improve security and privacy is discussed [4]. Security and privacy challenges in federated learning, discussing attacks and future research to enhance FL system's robustness are analysed [6]. Comparison of edge and cloud computing for IoT applications, discussing their roles, their advantages, and limitations in modern distributed computing scenarios [8]. An overview of federated learning and its strategies, applications, tools, and future research directions across many domains are discussed [10]. Federated learning's role in healthcare and its pipeline, applications, and challenges in ensuring privacy and efficiency are analysed [11]. Edge computing's effect on distributed systems, discussing its architectures, benefits, and challenges are analysed [13]. Edge computing concepts, applications, and future directions, emphasizing its advantages over traditional cloud computing are explored [14]. Industry views on edge computing and its changing relationship with cloud computing are analysed [17]. Edge computing's application in Internet of Things (IoT), focusing on architecture and challenges are discussed [18]. A loss decomposition method to handle data heterogeneity in federated learning, improving model performance across diverse datasets is proposed [19]. Federated learning's performance in edge computing environments, analysing computational efficiency and accuracy is evaluated [20].

div.head: IV.METHODOLOGY
div.p: This approach uses Federated Learning and Edge Computing (FLEC) for healthcare analytics, making sure that local model is trained in edge devices while allowing data privacy [1]. Fig. 1 shows the flow chart used to explain the FLEC methodology. A simulated dataset is used for initial model validation and a controlled environment testing of FLEC's accuracy, loss, response times, and alert mechanism. Future work will include real-world dataset containing missing values and outliers.
1. Data Compression: Data is size-reduced before being sent to the cloud, adding delays.
FLEC: FL is applied at edge devices, decreasing response time.

Performance is improved by using deep learning models that lower computational overhead without compromising accuracy. Federated aggregation boosts model performance, and using a better optimizer algorithm like Adam enables faster training. Reliability is enhanced by using decentralized model updates, which reduce single points of failure and ensure robustness [3]. Alerts are validated with anomaly detection, and maintaining network connectivity makes the system suitable for healthcare applications.

Training and evaluation: The model trains for three rounds with three epochs each with the FL server aggregating updates every round for each device. Fig. 2 shows the report of FLServer after receiving updates from Edge1 and Edge2, Fig. 3 shows the report of FLClient (Edge1) after training and generating alerts, and Fig. 4 shows the report of FLClient (Edge2) after training and generating alerts. VI. RESULTS

The key findings from TABLE I and Fig. 5 include: Response time comparison in emergency scenarios: The FLEC system processed the simulated ECG patient data and had a faster response time compared to other computing paradigms, making it a viable solution during emergency scenarios. Accuracy (Last Epoch per Round):
• Edge1: In Fig. 3, it achieves 1.000 accuracy in the last epoch for all three rounds, showing perfect score. This shows that the model is learning data patterns properly.
• Edge2: In Fig. 4, it starts with 0.65 in round 1 but improves to 1.000 in rounds 2 and 3, showing significant learning progress.

div.head: VII. CONCLUSION
div.p: Abnormal vitals like high heart rate, low oxygen, abnormal temperature can be detected by FLEC and alerts are triggered. By locally processing data, it ensures faster response times without dependency on cloud [11]. Compared to Data Compression, Fog and Cloud Computings, FLEC gives quicker alerts and upgrades emergency responses. This makes FLEC the most efficient answer for emergency alerts and on-time intervention during important health situations like heart attacks. By each training round, FLEC also has shown increasing/stabliized accuracy as well as reduction in loss, making it ideal for emergency sitations in healthcare domain. Frequent transmissions of large model updates over small networks like 4G, Wi-Fi, or limited IoT bandwidth increase delays. Some edge devices may take longer to train than others, causing outdated updates and inconsistent aggregation of updates. More frequent model updates increase data transmission, causing congestion and slowing down real-time processing [1]. Since updates happen in rounds, real-time updates in patient vitals, like sudden drop in oxygen levels may not be immediately reflected in the next global model update. Low-power devices may not have enough computational capacity to quickly adjust models for realtime decision-making. By the time the updated model is deployed, the patient's condition may have already changed, leading to outdated or incorrect alerts. The future scope of FLEC is vast, especially in healthcare. A simulated dataset is used to analyse FLEC's performance and its model evaluation to ensure a controlled environment to test FLEC's accuracy, loss, response times, and alert mechanism. While the simulated dataset allows for controlled testing, real world scenarios introduce challenges like network congestion, hardware failures and missing or inaccurate patient vital values. Future work will include using real-world dataset testing to evaluate FLEC's working. Enhancing privacybased AI by allowing decentralized model training on edge devices, reducing transmission costs and latency can be made [17]. It can use real-time making of decisions in healthcare by providing instant patient alerts while ensuring data security. Future advancements may use blockchain for improved security, optimize allocation of resources, and improve model efficiency for lowfunctioning devices [20]. With 5G and AI, FLEC can cover large networks, helping in intelligent transmission and AI that is personalized, making it an important component of future intelligent computing.

figure.figDesc: Implementing federated learning and edge computing: The Flower framework works in FL by training models on edge devices locally, sharing only weight updates with a central server/FLServer, like a local laptop or a Jetson Nano [20]. The global model, which is the aggregation of all the updates from the edge devices done by FLServer, is created in the FLServer and updated over three rounds, and then sent back to edge devices [11]. This reduced loss (how poorly the model is performing during training) and stabilized accuracy, proving FLEC's improvement. In FL, the Flower framework allows for local model training in all edge devices/clients without sharing raw data [10]. FedAvg algorithm trains local models on these clients and averages their weights to update the global model in the FLServer [1]. 3. Patient alert system: Edge devices made alerts for abnormal values by monitoring vitals. This system allowed for quicker responses [10]. Performance comparison with other methods: FLEC's response time is contrasted with other computing techniques for emergency responses using simulated ECG training data that simulated 10,000 heart rate samples (60 to 200 bpm) and is stored in a pandas data frame. Heart rates more than 180 bpm are shown as abnormal. A Matplotlib bar chart visualizes the response times of the different methods. Fog Computing: Training happens at a mediator node (for example an edge gateway), increasing response time [14]. Cloud Computing: Training is centralized, leading to increased response time [13].
